activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Ruby went to the garden center with Dad. It was a big, noisy place. Trucks rumbled by the pots. Ruby picked out little plants. She got tomatoes, carrots and beans.

At home, Dad dug the dirt. Ruby planted every row. Then she had a problem. "Where did the tomatoes go?" she asked. She could not remember. All the rows looked the same. Only tiny green leaf tips showed in the soil.

Then Ruby had an idea. They went back to the garden center. Ruby found small sticks and drew a tomato on one. Dad wrote the word too. They pushed the stick into the dirt by the tomato row. A label stuck in the soil shows what was planted in each spot. Ruby made a carrot label. She made a bean label. "Now we know who lives here," she said.

Soon the plants grew tall. Ruby read each label. The tomatoes came up by the tomato stick. The carrots came up by the carrot stick. Ruby watered them and smiled. "Hello, little tomatoes," she said.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story: Carter stood in the kitchen with Mama. On the counter was his little toy slide. His toy pig wanted to go down. Carter put the pig at the top. "Whee!" he said. The pig slid down on its head. Thump! It fell off at the bottom. Carter tried again. Thump again. "Hmm," said Carter. "What if the pig moves the other way?" He turned the pig around. Now the pig's feet went first. The pig slid down and landed softly on its feet. It did not fall. Carter clapped. "Feet first!" he said. Then he heard a sizzle. Mama was at the stove. The pan was hot. Carter stayed back and watched from his chair. The pancake bubbled and flipped. "Hot pan, cold milk," said Mama, handing him his cup. Carter drank his milk and slid the pig down again, feet first, all the way.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Felix stood in the band room. A big drum sat on the floor. He wanted to play it.

Felix hit the drum. Boom! He laughed. Then he saw papers on the stand. They had little dots and lines. "What are these?" Felix asked.

Miss Kay smiled. "Those are notes," she said. "Written music uses notes to show which sounds to play." She pointed at one note. Felix hit the drum for that note. Boom! She pointed at a little note. Felix tapped soft. Bum. She pointed at a big note. Felix hit hard. BOOM!

A bird sat outside the window. It seemed to like the big notes. It puffed up and sang.

Felix played the dots one by one. Slow. Then fast. One note made a small sound. One note made a big sound. He tried again. And again. Miss Kay waited and smiled.

At the end, Felix hit the last note. BOOM! The bird flew up and sang loud. Felix raised his drumsticks. "Again!" he said.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Milo pushed the library door. The door had a big sign on it. Milo pointed at the sign. "What do those words say?" he asked. His mom read them out. "They say PUSH." Milo pushed, and the door opened. He laughed.

Milo wanted a book about a big red truck. He walked past the busy desks. He walked past a shelf with a label. The label said TRUCKS. "Mom, this says trucks!" said Milo. "Yes, it does," said Mom. "The words tell us what is inside." Milo pulled out a box of books. The box had words too. Those words said TRUCKS as well.

Milo opened a book. He started at the back page. Mom sat down next to him. She turned the book around. She flipped the pages, one by one, from the front. On the first page was a red truck under a tree. "There it is!" said Milo. He put his finger under the words. Mom read them out loud. "Big red truck," she read. A boy ran by, and a puppy began to chase him. Milo stayed on the rug. He turned to page two.

"Read the next words," said Milo.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Logan stood by the big hotel pool. The water was blue and shiny. His dad held his hand. "I want to swim," said Logan. "But my feet don't touch." He felt worried.

Dad walked into the water with him. It was warm on Logan's toes. "Hold the edge of the pool," said Dad. Logan grabbed the cool wall with both hands. He held on tight. "Now kick your legs," said Dad. Logan kicked and kicked. His legs made big splashes. The water went splash, splash, splash. Droplets flew up and landed on Dad's nose. Dad laughed and wiped his face. "You kicked me!" he said. Logan giggled. His legs felt strong.

A cute rubber duck floated by. It was the color yellow. It bobbed up and down in Logan's splashes. Logan kicked more, and the duck wiggled away. Dad smiled. "Kick, kick, kick," said Logan. He held the wall and kicked all the way to the steps. Dad lifted him out and wrapped him in a big soft towel. "Again tomorrow?" asked Dad. "Yes!" said Logan.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Cooper went to the ice rink with Mom, Dad and his friend Leo. The big game was starting! The skaters zoomed past so fast. One skater bumped another skater hard. The boy fell down on the ice.

Cooper saw a man in a striped shirt raise his arm. The whizzing stopped. The game stopped too! "Who is that?" Cooper asked Dad. Dad said, "That is the referee."

Cooper watched the referee all game long. A skater hit the puck with his stick too high. The referee saw it. He raised his arm again. The game stopped again! The referee watched and watched. When a player broke a rule, the referee saw it every time.

Cooper clapped his mittens. "He has eyes like a robot!" he said. The referee even waved at him.

After the game, Cooper took off his smelly boots. He asked Mom to color a referee on his picture. He drew the striped shirt with black and white. "He watches the game," Cooper said. "He makes the rules work!" Then he held his picture up high for everyone to see.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Grayson ran to the playground. He held Mama's hand. "Stay close to me," said Mama. Grayson kept his hand in hers.

The sun was up. It made the slide hot. Grayson put his hand near it. "Ouch, hot," he said. He pulled his hand back. Mama touched the slide first. "Too hot today," she said. Grayson slid on the cool slide instead. The cool slide felt good on his legs.

Grayson saw a shiny can by the fence. He reached for it. "Wait," said Mama. "We do not touch cans. A grown-up picks them up." Mama picked up the can with a bag. She put it in the bin. Grayson clapped. He liked to help keep the playground clean.

After the playground, they went home for pizza. "A real big slice," said Grayson. He took a bite. Yum.

Then it was bath time. Grayson wanted to jump in. But he remembered the hot slide. He stopped at the tub. "Mama, you check first," he said. Mama put her hand in the water. "It is warm, not hot," she said. Grayson touched the water with one toe. Warm, like a hug. He climbed in slowly and smiled. "Warm water," he said. "Just right."

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandpa came to stay at Jaxon's house. They played in the backyard all week. They made a big pile of leaves. They found a toy snake under the swing. "Is it real?" Jaxon asked. "No, it is pretend," Grandpa said. "I was afraid for a minute!"

Then the week was over. Grandpa put his bag in the car. He waved. The car went down the road. Jaxon felt like crying. "Can I see Grandpa again?" he asked his mom. "Yes," she said. "We can call him on the phone. We can see him on a video call. Or we can send him a letter."

Jaxon got his crayons. He drew Grandpa and the toy snake. Mom put the picture in an envelope. She wrote Grandpa's name on it. Then they walked to the big blue mailbox together. Jaxon pushed the envelope in. It fell down, out of sight. "Go fast, letter," said Jaxon.

story:
Sienna went to Grandpa's house. Then Grandpa said, "Time for your first haircut!" They walked to the salon down the street.

Sienna sat in the big chair. She slid down, down, down. The chair was too big! The hairdresser could not reach her hair. "Hmm," said Sienna. "I think I am too small." Grandpa laughed. "You are just right. The chair is too big."

The hairdresser brought something over. It was a little seat. "A booster seat," she said. "Little ones sit on it so I can reach their hair." Sienna sat on the booster seat. Up, up, up she went. Now she was tall like a mountain!

The hairdresser snipped. Snip, snip, snip. Grandpa made a silly face. "Your curls look tight and bouncy," he said. Sienna looked in the mirror. "I see a big girl!" she said. Grandpa clapped his hands.

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Jacob skipped into the kitchen. He could smell the warm bread. Grandma set the big bowl on the table.

"Time for the blessing," said Grandpa.

Jacob did not know what to do. Grandpa folded his hands. He bowed his head. Jacob peeked. He saw Grandpa's eyes were closed. Jacob peeked at Grandma. Her head was bowed too. Her eyes were closed.

"Thank you for the bread," Grandpa said. "Thank you for the snow outside. Thank you for Jacob."

Jacob peeked again. Two grandmas, two grandpas, all with closed eyes. He counted them. One, two, two again.

Now it was soup time. Jacob folded his little hands. He bowed his head. He closed his eyes tight. But then he peeked one more time. Grandpa was peeking too! Grandpa smiled at him.

"Big soup!" said Jacob. His spoon went clink, clink in the bowl.

"Eat it all up," said Grandpa. "Even the ugly brown carrots."

Jacob laughed and took a big bite.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Lillian was looking for Bunny. Bunny was lost. "Where can Bunny be?" she asked. Bunny was not on the bed. Bunny was not in the toy box. Lillian looked under her shirt on the chair. No Bunny there.

Then she saw something shiny. It was a little toy car. It was her brother Ben's car. Ben was looking sad. He had lost his car. Lillian picked up the car. She wanted to play with it. But it was Ben's. She ran to him. "Here is your car," she said. Ben smiled big. He hugged the car.

"Now I help you," said Ben. They looked together. "Where can Bunny be?" they asked. They looked in the basket. They looked in the hall. Ben peeked under the blanket on the couch. Something soft was there. It was Bunny! Bunny had been sleeping under the warm blanket, not in the cold toy box at all.

Lillian held Bunny close. "Thank you, Ben," she said. Ben rolled his car on the floor. Vroom, vroom. Lillian sat down next to him. She patted Bunny's ears. "Good night, Bunny," she whispered. "No more hiding."

story:
Oliver walked home with a small cage. Inside was his first pet, a white rabbit. "Hello, Pip," said Oliver. Pip had soft fur and long ears.

At home, Oliver fed Pip a carrot. He cleaned the cage with Dad. Then Oliver ran to the table for his snack. "Wait," said Dad kindly. "Wash your hands first." Oliver looked at his hands. They had rabbit fur and bits of hay on them. He ran back to the sink. He washed with soap and warm water, and Dad helped with the faucet. His hands were clean and nice now.

Oliver sat down and ate his apple slices. "Pip is a good pet," he said. "But my hands needed a wash." Dad smiled and gave Pip a fresh carrot. Pip nibbled it down to the very end, and Oliver laughed.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Florence ran to the shape table at school. She wanted to make a picture for her mom. There were squares and triangles in a big box. There were rectangles too.

Tom held up a tiny button. "This can't be a circle," he said. "The clock is a circle. Look how big it is!" Florence took the button. She held it near the big clock on the wall. Both were round. Both had no corners. "Look, Tom," she said. "Big circle, tiny circle. They are both circles." Tom smiled big. "A tiny circle is still a circle!" he said.

Florence paid her teacher one sticker for some paper. Then she glued the button on top. It became a bird sitting in a paper nest. Around it she put a square house and a red triangle roof. "Mom will love it," she said, and she kept it safe under her arm all the way home.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Charlie woke up and ran to the window. Snow was everywhere. "A snow day!" said Dad. "Let's go out after breakfast."

Charlie put on his boots and his red hat. His mittens had a hole, so one thumb could peek out. They walked to the quiet street. It was empty except for snow.

"I want a snowman," said Charlie. He patted the snow. The ball fell apart. He patted again. It fell apart again. "Try again," said Dad. So Charlie tried again, slow and patient.

Later, the sun came out. The snow felt a little wet now. Charlie patted a big ball. It stuck together! "It's packing!" he said. He rolled it and rolled it.

They made a tall snowman with a carrot nose. Charlie put his ear close to the snowman. "He is quiet," said Charlie. Dad laughed. "Let's make another one tomorrow."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Carter sat on the big soft couch. Grandma and Uncle Ben sat near him. Friends came over too. The big game was on TV. It was ice hockey.

Carter looked for the ball. He did not see one. "Where is the ball?" he asked. Uncle Ben pointed at the ice. "Look at the flat disc," he said. "It is called a puck." The players had long sticks. They hit the puck with the sticks. The puck slid fast across the cold ice.

Carter held his toy stick. He tapped a round coin on the rug. The coin slid under the coffee table, just like the puck. "I hit it like they do!" he said. Grandma laughed and helped him find the coin. On the TV, a player hit the puck into the net. The room cheered. Carter clapped his hands. "Thank you for the puck," he said to Uncle Ben. The clock on the wall showed it was almost bedtime, but Carter watched one more play, his coin warm in his little hand.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Jasper sat very still in the backyard. He wanted to name his five senses. Mama said, "Close your eyes. What can you hear?" Jasper listened. "A bird!" he said. "I hear it with my ears." Then he heard a dog bark. His ears heard that too. Ears were for hearing. He had one sense done.

Next, Jasper opened his eyes. "I see the bright sun," he said. "I see with my eyes." Two senses done. Mama gave him a strawberry. Jasper ate it. "Yum! I taste with my tongue." Three done. Then he touched the warm grass. "I feel with my hands," he said. Four done.

One sense was left. Jasper could not think of it. He sniffed and sniffed. Then he smelled cookies! "Mama, you bake cookies," he said. "I smell with my nose. That is five!" He ran to the kitchen. But the cookies were not done yet. Mama had only just mixed the dough. Jasper laughed. His nose knew before his eyes did. "Smell wins today," said Mama, and she handed him the spoon to lick.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Ruby sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. She wanted to feel brave today. The doctor came in with a smile.

"Hello, Ruby!" said the doctor. "Let's check your eyes. What do you see?" Ruby saw a picture of a duck. "A duck!" she said. Her eyes did that.

Then the doctor rang a little bell. Ding, ding! Ruby's ears heard it. "Loud!" she said, and she laughed.

The doctor held out a sticker that smelled like strawberries. Ruby's nose knew it right away. "I smell berries!" she said.

Then Ruby got a tiny cup with a sweet juice to drink. Her tongue tasted it. "Yummy!" she said.

"Now hold out your hand," said the doctor. She gave Ruby a small ice cube. Ruby touched it. "Cold, cold!" she cried. She dropped the ice cube right into her cup. It clinked.

The doctor listened to Ruby's neck and back with a soft tool. It went bump, bump. "That is your heart," the doctor said.

"You did great," the doctor said. Ruby got a shiny star sticker. She stuck it on her shirt. "I did it!" said Ruby.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Joseph ran out to the playground. It was a sunny day. The sun was bright. Joseph made a little face. He squinted and squinted.

"I can't see," said Joseph. His teacher Miss Ana heard him. She held up a sun hat. "Try this," she said. Joseph reached up and put it on. The hat sat over his eyes. The bright sun did not hurt now. He could see the slide. He could see his friend Sam.

The wind blew Sam's coat open. It was a windy day too. "Hold my hand," said Joseph. They walked to the slide together. Sam smiled at him.

"Nice hat," said Sam. Joseph tipped the sun hat down like a bow. Then he ran to the slide, fast, all the way to the top.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Penelope was playing in the backyard. She had three little toy cars. She wanted them to go fast. She pushed the blue car down the path. She pushed the yellow car past the red car. But the cars kept bumping into each other. That was the problem. Her cars needed a way to stop.

Then Penelope looked at the picnic table. There was a red apple and a green apple. Mom had just wiped the table, so it was clean. Penelope picked up both apples. She held up the red apple. "Stop," she said. Dad laughed and parked his toy truck. He held Penelope's hand like they do at the crossing, and they pretended to walk.

Then Penelope held up the green apple. "Green means go," said Dad. The blue car zoomed by. The yellow car zoomed by. When the red apple went up, every car stopped. When the green apple went up, every car went. Penelope made the red car wait a long time. Dad tapped his foot and laughed.

At the end, Penelope rolled the cars off the path. She got the little broom to sweep the crumbs away. The path was clean again. She put the red apple and the green apple back on the table. Then she held up the green apple one more time and shouted, "Go!"

activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Livia ran to the door in her socks. "Shot day!" she called. "Let's go, let's go!"

At the doctor's office, Mom sat down in a big chair. Livia sat next to her. There were chairs everywhere, and families in every one.

"When is my turn?" Livia asked.

"We wait here," said Mom. "The nurse will call your name at that door."

Livia watched the door. A nurse opened it. "Ben!" she called. A boy hopped up and ran in. The door shut.

"Next will be me!" said Livia.

A baby cried. A man read a book. Livia kicked her feet, fast, fast, fast.

Then the door opened. The nurse looked at her paper. "Livia!" she called.

Livia jumped up. "That is me!"

In the little room, the nurse tapped Livia's arm. "One quick pinch," she said.

Livia squeezed Mom's hand. The nurse pressed a tiny sticker onto her arm.

"All done," said the nurse.

"Already?" Livia laughed. She looked at her arm. There was the sticker, a shiny red star.

"Can we come back next week?" asked Livia.

Mom laughed and gave her a big hug. "Next time we wait in the big chairs again," she said.

"Good," said Livia. "I like waiting. My name always comes."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Cooper ran onto the soccer field. His team wore blue shirts. He kicked the ball to his friend Sam. Then the other team scored. The other team scored again. The game was over. Cooper's team lost. Cooper sat down on the grass. He did not want to talk. His mouth was dry, so he took a big drink of water.

The coach blew the whistle. "Line up, everyone," she said. "We say good game now." Cooper stood at the end of the line. The blue team and the red team made a long line together. Each player walked past and tapped hands. "Good game," said a red shirt boy. "Good game," said Cooper. "Good game," said a girl with a pretty red bow.

Then it was Cooper's turn again at the last red player. It was the boy who had scored. The boy smiled. "Nice kicks," he said. Cooper smiled too. The grumpy feeling went away, like clouds going away. The red team waved. The blue team waved back. Cooper picked up the ball and hugged it all the way to the car. "Good game," he said to the ball.

"See, this is my party invitation. It says the party is here, at the bowling alley. And it says three o'clock. That is when we start!" Milo smiled. "So we came to the right place."

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Jaxon sat in the family car. He was going to get his very first haircut. "You will look so handsome," said Mom. The sun did shine on Jaxon's hair. Jaxon patted his head. "One, two, three curls," he said. Mom laughed and parked the car.

At the salon, a lady named Rosa put a cape on Jaxon. Then she picked up her scissors. She cut one curl, then two curls, then three curls. Snip, snip, snip. Jaxon sat very still.

Soon Jaxon began to wiggle. He wiggled his shoulders. He rubbed his neck. "My neck feels funny," he said. Rosa saw the tiny bits of cut hair sitting on his neck. She took her soft brush. She brushed one bit away, then two bits, then three bits. The funny feeling went away. Jaxon sat still again.

"There," said Rosa. "One, two, three curls gone." Jaxon looked in the mirror. His hair was short and neat. Mom gave him a thumbs up. "Happy hair day," said Rosa. Jaxon grinned and patted his smooth neck.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Rosalie ran to the art room. "I want to paint today!" she said.

Miss Tam put out three pots. "This is red," she said. "This is blue. This is yellow." Rosalie pointed at each pot. "Red, blue, yellow," she said. She was so happy.

Rosalie dipped her brush in red. She painted a big red circle. Then she dipped the same brush in blue. Her circle turned purple! She jumped up. "Look! Look! I made purple!" She painted more and more.

When the bell rang, Rosalie wanted to run and play. But Miss Tam said, "Wait. Let's wash the brushes." Rosalie helped. They dipped each brush in water. The water turned pink, then grey. They laid the brushes flat on the tray to dry.

The next day, Ben had left his brush in the yellow pot. He tried to paint, but the brush was stiff and hard. "It won't bend," he said. Rosalie held up her clean, soft brush. "Mine bends! We washed it with water and let it dry."

Then Rosalie mixed yellow and red. Orange! She laughed out loud. "Orange is my favourite!" She painted a big orange sun with a soft, clean brush.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Lena wanted to read a book to Bear. She sat on the small red mat. She picked a book about a duck. She held it up for Bear to see.

"Look, Bear," said Lena. But the duck looked funny. The duck was upside down. All the little words were upside down too.

"Turn it around," said Mia, her friend. Lena turned the book around. Now the duck stood on his feet. Now the words sat flat and neat.

Lena opened the front cover. "This is the front," she said. She turned one page, then the next page. "The duck has a spoon," said Lena. "He eats his soup. Yum."

Mia laughed and kicked her feet. "Read more," she said.

Lena held the book up high. "The end," said Lena. "Now you, Bear." She put the book in Bear's paws. Bear's book was upside down. Lena turned it around for him.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Naomi picked a book for bedtime. She wanted to know who made up the story inside. The cover had words on it. She did not know what they said.

"Who made this story?" she asked Dad.

Dad pointed to the words. "This name is the author," he said. "The author is the person who wrote the words of the book." Naomi touched the letters. One by one, she counted them. "Four little letters," she said. "Words that tell a name!"

Dad opened the book at the front. He read page one, then page two. Naomi turned the next page herself. The story grew and grew, like magic from the kitchen making popcorn.

One page was missing! Naomi frowned. "Where did page three go?" Dad looked. The page had stuck to page four. Naomi peeled it apart, slow and careful. There it was, a beautiful picture of a red boat.

Naomi hugged the book. "The author wrote the boat," she said. Dad laughed. "Don't forget the waves," he said. Naomi patted the cover. "Good night, author," she whispered. "Good night, boat."

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Florence stood in the backyard. Her brother Ben had a big red ball. He threw it high up in the air.

"Watch me," said Ben. He caught the ball with one hand. He was big, and his hand was big too.

Florence wanted to catch the ball. Ben tossed it to her gently. She held out one small hand. The ball hit her fingers. Bump! It fell on the grass. Florence picked it up and tried again. One hand, bump, drop. One hand, bump, drop.

Then Florence held out both hands. Ben threw the ball. Florence caught it! Both hands held the big ball tight. She laughed and jumped up and down.

"Now the hoop," said Ben. He put a hoop on the grass. Florence threw her beanbag. It went in! Then the wind began to blow. A leaf landed on the hoop like a little hat.

Florence threw the beanbag again. It bounced off the leaf hat and rolled away. Florence and Ben chased it around the yard. They laughed so much that the dog woke up from being asleep under the tree. The dog grabbed the beanbag and ran.

"That is my soup day beanbag," said Ben. "Mama sewed it from soup beans."

Florence held out both hands. "Drop it," she said. The dog dropped the beanbag right into her hands. Florence smiled. Two hands work for beanbags too.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Jules wanted to help make bread. Mama said, "You can watch. The oven is hot." Jules stood on his spot by the counter.

Mama mixed flour and water. Jules heard the spoon knock, knock against the bowl. His ears heard that sound. Then Mama opened the yeast. Jules used his nose to sniff. "It smells funny," he said. "What is that smell?" Mama said, "That is the yeast. Smell it again." Jules sniffed. His nose had two openings called nostrils. "Say that word," said Mama. "Nos-trils," said Jules.

Mama gave him a small ball of dough. He touched it with his hands. It was soft and squishy. "Can I see my nostrils?" he asked. Mama held up a shiny spoon. Jules looked into it. He saw his own nose. "One, two," he counted. "Two holes!" He laughed. "They are at the top of my nose!"

Mama put the bread in the oven. Jules waited. It was hard to wait. Soon the kitchen smelled warm and sweet. The timer rang, and Mama took the bread out. She cut one slice. Jules took a little bite with his mouth. "Mmm," he said. "It tastes so good. My nose smelled it first!" He held the slice in both hands and took another big bite.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Evan stood by the school gate. It was his first day. He wanted to find the toy trucks fast. So he ran ahead on the path. But he got stuck behind a big red door. It was too heavy to open alone.

His teacher came. She smiled and pushed the door. Light from the sun came in. "Time to walk with us," she said. All the children stood one behind another. They made a long line, like train cars.

Evan found his spot. He held the rope handle. The whole line walked together, slow and steady. Past the slide. Past the swing. At the door to the classroom, everyone stopped. One boy tried to break away and run inside. "Not yet," said the teacher. She opened the door wide.

Evan walked in with his line. There, on the mat, sat the trucks. "I found them!" he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Milo ran to Grandma's big chair. Grandma had a cloth bag on her lap.

"We will play a game," said Grandma. "Put your hand in. Do not peek. Tell me what you feel."

Milo put his hand in the bag. He felt something round and smooth. "A ball!" he said. "It is a red ball!"

"Open your eyes wide and look," said Grandma.

Milo pulled out the ball. It was not red. It was blue! He laughed. "I could not tell. My fingers felt the ball. But my fingers did not tell me the color. I had to look with my eyes."

"Try again," said Grandma.

Milo shut his eyes. He put his hand back in the bag. He felt something long and smooth. "A crayon!" he said. "Is it green?"

He looked. The crayon was yellow! "I must look to see," said Milo. "My fingers cannot see colors."

Grandma clapped. Then she yawned a big yawn. "Time for my nap," she said softly.

Milo did not want Grandma to be sleepy. He found her soft blanket. He put it on her lap. "Now try one more ball," he whispered.

Grandma put her hand in the bag. "Round and smooth. Is it yellow?"

"You have to look!" said Milo. Grandma pulled it out. The ball was green!

"My eyes see it," said Grandma. "But first, my nap." She closed her eyes. Milo tiptoed out with his blue ball.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Elizabeth did not want to sleep. She wanted to play all night.

"Can I stay up, Mama?" she asked.

"Just a little longer," said Mama. "Then bath, pajamas, bed."

Elizabeth sat in the warm bath. She counted the bubbles. One, two, three. Mama washed her hair. Then Mama helped her get dressed in soft pajamas. Elizabeth zipped her own sleep sack. Ziiiip!

Mama tucked her in, safe and cozy. "Good night, Elizabeth."

In the morning, Elizabeth woke up. She ran to her blocks. She built a tall tower. She jumped and danced and sang.

The next night, Elizabeth asked, "What if I stay up all night?"

"You can try," said Mama.

Elizabeth stayed up very late. Her eyes got heavy. In the morning, she could not build. She could not jump. She was too tired to play.

"Sleeping at night gives your body rest for the next day," said Mama.

So that night, Elizabeth took her bath. She put on her pajamas. She zipped her sleep sack. One, two, three, good night.

In the morning, she built the tallest tower yet.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Iris put on her red socks at school. She liked getting dressed all by herself. Then it was time for a crunchy snack. Iris ate apple slices. Crunch, crunch, crunch.

After snack, Iris needed the toilet. She went into the little bathroom. She closed the door. She used the toilet. Then she ran out fast to play.

Teacher Mia called, "Iris! Come and look." The toilet water was still there. "You forgot to flush," said Teacher Mia. Iris asked, "What do I do now?" Teacher Mia smiled. "After using the toilet, we flush," she said.

Iris pushed the handle. Whoosh! The water swirled away. "And then we wash our hands," said Teacher Mia. Iris turned on the sink. She washed her hands with soap. Bubbles, bubbles!

Later it was nap time. Iris lay on her little mat. She thought about the whoosh. First flush, then wash. First flush, then wash. "Will we wash after lunch too?" she asked herself. "Yes," she whispered. "Hands get washed a lot."

Her eyes closed slowly, and her red socks peeked out from under the blanket.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Leo planted little seeds in pots on the balcony. He planted lettuce, carrots and one big sunflower. His friend Mia came over to see. "It looks like a tiny farm," she said.

Every morning Leo gave the pots a drink from his orange watering can. Then one hot day, Leo played all day at Mia's house. He forgot to water his plants. When he came home, the lettuce was drooping. Its leaves hung down like sad little ears. "Oh no," said Leo.

Leo ran to get his watering can. He gave the droopy lettuce a big drink. The next morning, the lettuce stood up tall. "Water makes you wake up!" said Leo. Mia laughed. "You are a good plant friend," she said. Leo watered the carrots too, just in case.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Alexis ran to Grandma's house. He ran fast through the yard. His shoes went clap, clap, clap on the porch. Inside there was a new baby. The baby was his new baby sister. She was small as a loaf of bread.

"Can I hold her now?" asked Alexis.

"Yes," said Grandma. "Big brothers wash their hands first."

Alexis looked at his hands. They had dirt on them. One hand had a smudge of mud. The other had grass stains. "My hands are not clean," he said. He held them up to show Grandma. "Look! My hands are all yucky."

Grandma laughed a little laugh. "Come with me," she said. She took him to the sink. She turned on the water. It was warm. Alexis made bubbles with the soap. The bubbles were big and shiny. He popped one on his nose. "Pop!" he said. Grandma said he was a silly boy. She said he was not a mean brother, just a messy one.

Then his hands were clean. They smelled like flowers. Grandma sat him in the big chair. She put a pillow on his lap. Then she set the baby sister on the pillow. The baby made a small sound. It sounded like a tiny sneeze.

"Hello, baby," said Alexis. "I am your big brother. I washed my hands for you." The baby grabbed his finger. Her hand was very small. Alexis smiled so big his cheeks hurt. "Grandma, she likes me!" he said. "She really works at holding on!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Aaron was at Grandma's house. Grandma was playing a game with him. "Show me your eyes," she said. Aaron pointed to his eyes. "Eyes see!" he said. "Show me your ears." Aaron wiggled his ears. "Ears hear!" Then the phone did ring, ring, ring. Grandma said, "That is the phone. Ears hear the ring." Aaron laughed and clapped.

"Now show me your nose," said Grandma. Aaron pointed to his nose. He sniffed and sniffed. Something smelled sweet. Something smelled warm. "I smell cookies!" said Aaron. "I do not see cookies," he said. He looked left. He looked right. No cookies. Was he wrong? Grandma smiled. "Follow your nose," she said.

Aaron sniffed and walked. He sniffed and walked. His nose led him to the kitchen. There sat Grandma's oven, all warm and shut tight. Grandma opened it with her big glove. Cookies! Aaron had smelled them before he could see them. "My nose knew first!" said Aaron. Grandma gave him a cookie. Aaron sniffed the cookie, then took a big bite. "Noses smell," he said, with crumbs on his chin.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Jasper stood at the painting table at school. He wanted to paint ten balloons. His teacher, Miss May, had hung up a counting song poster. "One, two, three, four, five," the children sang. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten," they sang next. Jasper tapped his brush and counted with them. He painted one red balloon, then two blue balloons, then three yellow ones.

Soon he had ten balloons on his paper. Then Miss May asked, "Can you write the number too?" Jasper wrote a 1 for one balloon. He wrote a 3 for three balloons. He wrote a 9 for nine balloons. Then he stopped. Ten felt big. He made a 1. He made a 0 next to it. He looked at Miss May. "Ten uses two numbers," she said with a smile. "A 1 and then a 0."

Jasper wrote 10 under his balloons. His friend Leo leaned over to look. "Ten has a 1 and a 0," said Jasper. Leo clapped his soft little hands. Jasper carried his painting to the wall. It would go home in his bag today. On the way, he passed the toy shelf. A toy truck sat there with a broken wheel. Jasper set his painting down gently. He pushed the truck to the fixing basket for Miss May. Then he picked up his ten balloons again and held them up high. "Ten!" he said. "A 1 and a 0."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Zoe went to the health clinic with her mom. A friendly nurse said, "Time to check you." Zoe stepped onto the big scale. She wiggled her toes. The numbers jumped up and down. "Why do the numbers jump?" Zoe asked. "Because you are moving," said the nurse.

Zoe tried again. She stood very still. She held her arms at her sides. The numbers stopped jumping. The scale showed how much she weighed. "The number stayed put!" Zoe said. "Yes," said the nurse. "Standing still helps."

Then the nurse said, "Now it is time for your shot." Zoe held her mom's hand. She stood still, just like on the scale. The nurse counted, "One, two, three." It was done. It hurt just a little bit.

"Did I do it?" Zoe asked. "You did it," said Mom. The nurse put a fun bandage on Zoe's arm. It had a garden on it, with flowers and a bunny. On the way out, Zoe pushed the door open by herself. "I stood still like a big girl," she said. Mom smiled and said, "You surely did."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Jaxson ran into the kitchen. He was still in his pajamas. He saw the cookie jar up high. "Cookies! Cookies!" he said.

Mom shook her head. "Cookies are not for breakfast," she said. "Breakfast is the first meal of the day. It comes first, before lunch and dinner."

Jaxson pouted. He wanted cookies. But then he heard his tummy rumble. Rumble, rumble. Mom laughed. "Let's pick a breakfast together. You can help."

Jaxson looked in the fridge. He found eggs. Mom cracked them. Jaxson stirred. Mom cooked them on the stove, and Jaxson watched from his chair. He put bread on his plate. He put a banana by it too.

After eating, Jaxson had a bath. The water was warm. Mom washed his hair. Then Jaxson got dressed in his blue shirt. He helped make the kitchen tidy.

That night, Dad read him a story. "What do we call the first meal of the day?" Dad asked. Jaxson grinned. "Breakfast!" he said. "But not cookies!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Zoe sat in the big waiting room. The chairs were blue and squeaky. She held her bunny tight. The room smelled like soap. A fish swam in a little tank. Zoe tapped the glass, and the fish swam away fast.

A nurse called, "Zoe, it is your turn." Zoe walked in slowly. She saw a small tray with a tiny needle. Her tummy felt tight. "But I am not sick," Zoe said. "Why do I need a shot?" The doctor smiled. "The shot helps protect your body from getting some sicknesses," she said. "It helps keep you well, so you can go to your class tomorrow."

Zoe looked at her bunny. "You can have one too, bunny," she whispered. She felt one quick pinch, like a tiny bug kiss. Then it was done. The doctor gave her a special bandage with stars on it.

Zoe picked a sticker from a basket. She chose a shiny red heart. On the way out, she skipped past the fish tank. "Bye, fish!" she said. "I am going back to my class tomorrow."

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Xavier was at school. Miss Ana held up a tablet. "We can draw on this," she said. Xavier wanted to draw a red sun.

He tapped the big button. The screen lit up. He clapped his hands. Miss Ana helped him find the drawing app. It had a sticky spot on it from someone's snack. She wiped it clean. Xavier tapped the app. It opened.

Now he needed red. He looked at the little colours on the screen. He tapped a blue dot. His line came out blue. "Not blue," said Xavier. His friend Lily pointed. "Tap the red one." He tapped the red colour. He drew his finger across the screen. A red line came out. He made a big round sun. It was all red.

"Time to put it away," said Miss Ana. Xavier pressed the button. The screen went dark. He put the tablet in the basket, all by himself. "Good job, Xavier," said Lily. Xavier smiled and waved at the basket.
